claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native oxide layer.
The formation and microstructural integrity of the native iron oxide layer govern whether Q235 retains corrosion protection in aggressive high-temperature salts.
The protective native oxide on Q235 is primarily Fe3O4.
A dense, adherent iron oxide layer formed at room temperature can protect Q235 against salt-induced corrosion.
At room temperature, the thin oxide layer passivates Q235 and retards further oxidation or salt attack.
Exposure or annealing at 700–900 °C causes grain coarsening in the protective oxide scale.
High-temperature exposure generates differential-expansion stresses and microcracks in the protective oxide scale.
High temperature accelerates oxide-scale growth on Q235.
Microcracking and reduced adherence cause oxide-scale spallation.
Damage and spallation of the scale allow aggressive salt to produce increased oxidation and higher corrosion rates.
Q235 samples retaining an intact, uniform oxide layer will exhibit lower mass loss and less severe corrosion morphology than high-temperature-pretreated samples with cracked oxide.
Untreated Q235 exposed to room-temperature salt retains its native oxide and receives moderate corrosion protection.
For low-alloy Q235 steel, the oxide scale is the main corrosion barrier.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when Mn or Cr alloying additions or engineered coatings produce different protective scales.
Corrosion behavior in aggressive salts can depend on the thermodynamic stability of corrosion products and salt impurities.
Mass change per unit area and cross-sectional EDS can reveal salt-induced material loss and attack depth.
Annealing in an inert atmosphere at 700–900 °C will deliberately modify the existing oxide without introducing additional environmental oxidation.

contradictions.description: The main intervention and conditions compare high-temperature salt exposure with a room-temperature salt test, thereby varying both pretreatment and exposure temperature. The falsification design instead says that annealed and room-temperature groups receive subsequent salt exposure under identical conditions. These are materially different control schemes.

The predicted outcome describes an intact oxide 'as seen in room-temperature tests,' whereas the falsification design does not clearly specify that the unannealed control remains at room temperature during salt exposure. Thus the temperature associated with the predicted reference is inconsistent or ambiguous.
